conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m so glad you’re here.  
I’d like to spend a few minutes with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied set of questions that helps us see how you’re feeling emotionally now that your baby has arrived. Nothing you share will leave this room unless you or your baby’s safety is at risk, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you.

We’ll go through ten questions, each about how you’ve felt in the past seven days. If any question feels hard to talk about, we can pause or adjust. Ready to start?

Over the past week, when you were able to sleep, how did you generally feel—pretty rested, or still exhausted, or somewhere in between?

Honestly, even when I do get a stretch of sleep, I wake up feeling like I never actually rested. My body’s heavy, my mind’s racing, and I’m already dreading the next feeding. I guess “exhausted” is the word, but it feels deeper than just tired—like I’m running on fumes every single day.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, most days nothing feels funny. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I half-smiled, but then I caught myself thinking, “What’s the point?” So I’d say “not so much now.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk around the lake, even just a quiet shower. Now… nothing sounds worth the effort. I’ll plan to meet someone and then cancel because it feels overwhelming and I’m sure I’ll just end up crying in the car. So, no, I’m not really looking forward to anything right now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty often. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not soothing her right, or my milk isn’t enough, or I missed some cue. Last night she wouldn’t settle and I just sat there rocking her, whispering “sorry” over and over, like I’d already failed her for life. I know in my head that babies cry, but the voice inside keeps saying, “You’re just not good at this.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… pretty much all the time. I’ll be folding her onesies and suddenly I’m sure she’s going to stop breathing in the crib, so I run in to check. Or I worry the formula I supplement with is poisoning her, or that a car will jump the curb when we’re on a walk. None of it makes sense, but I can’t turn the fear off—it just keeps looping.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… sometimes it hits out of nowhere. Like yesterday I was just giving her a bottle and suddenly my heart was racing, I couldn’t catch my breath, and I had to put her down in the crib so I could sit on the floor with my head between my knees. There wasn’t anything happening—no noise, nobody else in the house—but I felt like something awful was about to happen. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one thing—diaper, feeding, pumping—there are three more waiting. The laundry mountain, the dishes, the texts I haven’t answered. I’ll sit down for a second and hear her stir, and it’s like my chest tightens all over again. I keep thinking, “I can’t do all of this,” but I still get up and do it, so I guess I’m managing… barely.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head starts spinning with everything I did wrong that day—did I hold her enough, why did I snap at my mom, am I already ruining her—and then I’m wide awake. Some nights I just stare at the ceiling until the first morning feeding, or I drift off right before she wakes up. It’s like my body forgets how to shut off.
I have felt sad or miserable

That pretty much sums up most of my days. There’s this heavy, gray feeling that just sits on me. I’ll be changing her diaper and tears start coming out of nowhere. I keep thinking I should feel grateful—I’ve got this healthy baby—but instead I feel hollow, like I’m watching someone else’s life through fogged glass.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s like the tears are always right there. Sometimes it’s a full-on sob when I’m alone in the bathroom, sometimes just leaking while I rock her at 3 a.m. I cried in the grocery line yesterday because the cashier smiled at me and it felt kind, and that kindness just broke the dam. I’d say it’s been at least four or five times this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had thoughts like that. I feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels clouded by a heavy, gray sadness that follows you most days. Even simple pleasures-laughing at a meme, looking forward to coffee with a friend, or enjoying a quiet shower-seem out of reach, and you find yourself canceling plans because the effort feels overwhelming. You described constant, looping worries about your baby's safety, sudden panic that takes your breath away, and nights spent wide-awake reviewing every perceived mistake. Tears come easily, whether you're rocking your daughter or standing in a grocery line, yet you still gather the strength to keep caring for her because you desperately want to be the mom she deserves.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports minimal amusement and persistent anhedonia, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure and actively avoids previously enjoyable activities, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ("pretty often") and provides multiple vivid examples of feeling at fault for normal infant behavior, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive, irrational fears occurring "pretty much all the time" and feels unable to stop the looping thoughts, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness, catastrophic fear) that arose "out of nowhere" while feeding baby—classic unexpected panic attack matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days" and struggling to keep up, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive worries, lying awake for hours or until almost dawn—clearly "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness ('most of my days'), spontaneous tears, and emotional numbness—closely matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, easily triggered crying episodes (4-5 times in a week) indicating pervasive sadness consistent with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you well above the threshold of 13 that signals probable major depression requiring prompt evaluation. You endorse feeling sad or miserable most of the time, crying most days, loss of enjoyment in almost all activities, inappropriate guilt, anxiety and panic, and insomnia driven by rumination-five core symptoms that align closely with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. The intensity and frequency of these symptoms, plus significant impairment in daily functioning, warrant urgent referral for formal assessment and possible treatment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Ask your provider about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, or <med>serotonergic antidepressants</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Arrange practical help-partner, family, or postpartum doula-for night feeds and household tasks so you can get at least one 4-hour stretch of sleep
4. Use a simple daily mood log or app to track symptoms and share with your clinician at follow-up
5. Continue to voice any scary thoughts or urges; if they worsen or you ever feel unsafe with yourself or your baby, call 911, go to the nearest ED, or contact the 988 crisis line
6. Keep your baby's next pediatric visit; let the pediatrician know you're being evaluated for postpartum depression so the clinic can support both of you
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Epworth 10-item self-report

<sym>Symptoms endorsed</sym>
- Marked anhedonia (loss of laughter, anticipatory pleasure)
- Persistent low mood, frequent crying (≥ 4–5×/week)
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care
- Generalized anxiety & panic attacks (no clear precipitant)
- Sleep disruption secondary to ruminations
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to “get on top” of daily tasks
- No self-harm ideation

<sym>Pattern</sym>
High distress across mood, anxiety, and functioning domains; no safety concerns currently voiced.

Risk indicators: probable major depressive and anxiety symptoms post-delivery; impairment in self-care and infant care confidence; early identification recommended.
